title: Guitarist Frank Galandry and the names Storyville and the district
summary: Amacker calls Galandry a marvelous guitarist and explains that the red-light area was called Storyville or the district, and what going down the line meant.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Frank Galandry was one of the greatest guitar players I've ever known. You can follow. He's been dead about over 50 years ago, I imagine. He's formerly from New Orleans. He's a jazz player. He's one of the most marvelous guitar players I've ever known in my life. He's played all the sporting part of the district. They didn't call it Booker Ray then.
They called it Storyville then. They called it Storyville then.
Where did that name come from?

Storyville. They originated all from a lot of the pioneers, road setters, other sporting houses downtown. It was called Storyville then. And this Booker Ray is just this recent name. But that was called, in those years, 40, 50 years ago, was called Storyville. It's called Storyville.
Do they have any other names for it then?

Well, it's called the district. Storyville, and if he's talking to a man, either tell he's played in Storyville, I tell he's played in the district. One or the other. If he's in Storyville, I play in the district.
What did that mean when they said, I'm going down the line?

Well, a lot of sporting houses were down there then. Sporting girls have plays of all kinds, you know, so that's what they call it. Going down to see the sporting part of town, have a nice time with the girls. So they call that sporting part of town, going down the line then.
Going down the line, huh? I don't think I could go down the line all in one night, though. That would be quite a job.
